differences.title: 1. PROTOCOL & API
differences.leftDesc: Dragonfly speaks a Redis-style command surface, enabling drop-in use patterns like SET/GET plus Lua-like behaviors via compatibility layers. It also exposes cluster-like routing primitives for horizontal scaling and consistent hashing.
differences.rightDesc: Memcached implements a purpose-built text/binary protocol limited to straightforward get/set/add/replace/delete operations. This simplicity reduces surface area and parsing overhead, but complicates migration from Redis command patterns and feature parity.

differences.title: 2. SHARDING MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Dragonfly commonly supports server-side sharding patterns where keys map to shards using consistent hashing-like logic. That keeps request routing consistent across nodes and reduces application complexity when scaling cache capacity.
differences.rightDesc: Memcached deployments usually rely on client-side hashing (via libraries like libmemcached) to decide which server owns a key. Scaling requires rehashing behavior and careful client configuration to avoid hot shards or cache misses.

differences.title: 3. DATA EXPIRATION
differences.leftDesc: Dragonfly tracks TTL per entry and can expire keys without full scans, using background eviction mechanics plus lazy checks on access. This balances latency and memory reclaim for high churn workloads.
differences.rightDesc: Memcached stores an absolute expiration timestamp per item. It evicts via lazy expiration on reads plus periodic background cleanup, meaning expired keys might remain until accessed or reclaimed by the eviction loop.

differences.title: 4. EVICTION & PRESSURE
differences.leftDesc: Dragonfly uses in-memory allocation strategies designed to reduce fragmentation and supports eviction policies intended to handle hot keys and memory pressure more predictably under concurrent load.
differences.rightDesc: Memcached allocates memory in slab classes (size buckets) and evicts within the relevant slab when full. The slab mechanism lowers fragmentation but can yield uneven effective capacity across key sizes.

differences.title: 5. MULTI-CORE CONCURRENCY
differences.leftDesc: Dragonfly targets high throughput by aligning request processing with multi-core execution, reducing lock contention around hot data paths. It’s engineered to keep CPU pipelines busy under concurrent clients.
differences.rightDesc: Memcached historically uses a worker model where each server process handles requests efficiently but can require multiple instances to scale across cores. Cross-thread coordination is minimal, but scaling concurrency often means more daemons.

differences.title: 6. RESILIENCE & FAILOVER
differences.leftDesc: Dragonfly is built for production cache clusters with shard placement and reconfiguration patterns that minimize downtime impact. Clients typically tolerate transient misses while shards rebalance data availability.
differences.rightDesc: Memcached is inherently a best-effort cache without replication guarantees by default. On node loss, keys disappear until clients repopulate, so failover is operationally handled by reintroducing instances and warming caches.

differences.title: 7. USE CASE FIT
differences.leftDesc: Dragonfly fits teams migrating Redis-like caching semantics while pushing higher throughput and lower operational friction. It’s often chosen when you need more than basic get/set but still want in-memory latency.
differences.rightDesc: Memcached is a great fit for straightforward key/value caching where predictable latency and minimal complexity matter. Its limited command set keeps the hot path small, making it easy to deploy broadly.
